newsitem.title: UK: Funds short emerging targets to buy in '97 - Mobius.
newsitem.headline: Funds short emerging targets to buy in '97 - Mobius.

text.p: Global funds have missed their 1996 emerging market investment targets because of opportunities in developed markets and 1997 will see a new surge of buying, Mark Mobius, president of the Franklin Templeton Group said.

In an interview in London, Mobius, who now controls over $10 billion in 34 emerging market funds, said the pick-up would be a direct consequence of the rallies that have occurred in the U.S. and other mainstream equity markets.

"Clients have been overweight there but they realise they must diversify," said Mobius. "This is particularly true in the U.S. where institutional investors have not yet met the five or 10 percent emerging market targets they set two years ago."

He said the argument for emerging markets first deployed over 10 years ago was still intact -- developing markets provide strong growth, higher returns and risk-lowering diversification for global investors.
After a rocky 1996, emerging markets would rebound in 1997, even if U.S. interest rates rise. "But it depends of course on the size of any rate hike and what the news is alongside it."

Some markets highly correlated with the U.S., like Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan and Argentina, would be hit but this was "usually a temporary setback", he added. India, which is negatively correlated, could benefit, although other factors there such as poor liquidity still discouraged global investors.
Mobius said the trend towards privatisation in many emerging markets continued to be a strong lure, with more and more stocks being listed and market capitalisations growing.

"Contrary to most markets, supply here is not depressing demand but attracting fresh money as the markets deepen," he noted. "It is not a zero sum game...100 IPOs do not mean 100 less investments in other stocks, the base is just widening."

But privatisations did carry political risk because they usually involved painful downsizing. In Argentina, which he has just visited, unemployment is at 17 percent and many blame privatisation sell-offs.
"There is a certain danger that the political will (for economic reform) could be dissipated, especially if a country has elections coming up," he said.
"But it is mainly unions, set to lose power, complaining. Ordinary people are responding by creating service jobs for themselves, although these are often not within the tax net."
Among other trends for the coming year, Mobius said the robust growth in retail sales in emerging markets was sometimes outpacing overall economic growth.

"This indicates there is more money in the system than first appears. That is boosted with declining inflation, like in Brazil. We also notice that big global retailers (like France's Carrefour) are moving into emerging markets," he said.
For asset managers, though, the going is getting tougher. "When we first started it was relatively easy -- few people on the block and very few stocks," said Mobius.

"Now the amount of money in these markets is increasing dramatically and the whole process is much more intense. A 16 percent move in emerging markets this year would be a lot more than maybe 60 percent in 1993. There is a lot of money around."

He sees best value for 1997 in Hong Kong, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Turkey. In Asia, "prices have run away from us" but he describes the outloook for South Africa, where the company currently holds two percent of its assets, as "bright".
The rand may lose another five to 10 percent and the political risks are not fully factored into the market, which will bring valuations down to a more realistic level, he said.
Elsewhere, Russia has "reached a plateau".
"What global investors need there is deepening and lengthening, more shares and liquidity."
-- Caroline Allen, London newsroom +44 171 542 6414
